name: Century Tree

location.address: Texas A&M University main campus, beside the Academic Building (site of Old Main), College Station, TX 77843

access: Open outdoor campus grounds beside the Academic Building; no ticket, no gate seen in sources. Visitor parking rules on campus apply.
transport: On the central campus of Texas A&M; Aggie Spirit campus buses serve the Academic Building area. Not checked against a timetable.
story:
The crown of the Century Tree spreads about 101 feet, more than twice as wide as the tree is tall. Nobody wrote down when it was planted. A 1908 bulletin from the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station describes a live oak set out in 1891 on the hard-tramped parade ground, an 18-inch sapling that had reached 28 feet in sixteen years. In 2018 KBTX reported that the bulletin's photograph shows this tree beside Old Main, and a Texas A&M Forest Service forester calls it a good candidate. Before that match, the best guess was around 1900 or later. So it is somewhere between about 110 and 135 years old, and every account of it comes from the university or the local station.

Old Main burned in 1912. The oak outlived it, and its roots are said to have found a cistern under the lost building. About a decade ago it measured some 45 feet tall with a trunk nearly 11 feet round. Oak wilt struck trees nearby and has not been seen in this one; the grounds arborist pruned its deadwood and fed the soil after a nitrogen shortfall.

Campus tradition says a couple who walk beneath it together stay together, which is why people propose and marry here. In 2025 the university cloned it, rooting more than 40 copies.

It is young for this map. History and that crown are what earn it a place.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 101 feet across and more than twice the tree's height. It stands on its own beside the Academic Building, on the site of the Old Main that burned in 1912.

name: Houston Campsite Oak

location.address: Grapevine Springs Park, 700 S Park Road, Coppell, TX 75019

access: Public city park maintained by the City of Coppell; open 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset. Parking at the Coppell Senior & Community Center, 345 W. Bethel Road. The tree is marked with a sign.
transport: Car; about 26 km northwest of central Dallas. No public-transport walk established.
story:
In 1843 Sam Houston spent about six weeks camped under a post oak here, waiting to sign a peace treaty with Native nations. The City of Coppell, which looks after the park, calls the tree the Sam Houston Treaty Oak. Dallas County's account and the Coppell Historical Society agree on the outline: almost six weeks of waiting in 1843, and a treaty that was finally signed months later at Bird's Fort, near present-day Euless.

Not every telling matches. A student article puts the camp in 1836, and the state historical marker for the park places the treaty site near Arlington. Whether this particular trunk is the one Houston slept beneath is tradition rather than record. Nobody has published its age, its girth or its height either. If you know how old it is, tell us.

What is on record is that it is alive and doing well. A visitor who came in December 2019 found it bare, returned in spring 2020 to find it in full leaf, and called it healthy.

It grows in Grapevine Springs Park, 23 acres with features built by the Works Progress Administration. A sign marks it, so there is no guessing which oak carries the name. The park opens half an hour before sunrise and closes half an hour after sunset.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the sign that marks it, the one named tree in Grapevine Springs Park. It stands in the park at 700 S Park Road; parking is at the Senior & Community Center on W. Bethel Road.

name: Cart War Oak (Goliad Hanging Tree)

location.address: North lawn, Goliad County Courthouse, 127 N Courthouse Square, Goliad, TX 77963

access: Courthouse lawn on the town square; open grounds, no ticket. Courthouse hours not established.
transport: Car; Goliad is about 150 km southwest of Houston. No public transport established.
story:
For a quarter of a century, Goliad held court in the shade of this oak. The state historical marker beside it, as it has been quoted, says court sessions met here from 1846 to 1870, and that the tree was also used for hangings that no court ordered. The worst of them came in 1857, during the Cart War against Mexican cartmen. About 70 men were killed before the Texas Rangers intervened, and some of them were hanged from this tree.

Texas Escapes called it the Cart War Oak in 2001 and placed it on the north side of the courthouse lawn, where Texas Highways puts it too. Others know it as the Goliad Hanging Tree. The figures above are the marker's, known through quotation, and little else has been written about the tree, so read them as the marker's account rather than a full history.

The courthouse behind it is the Second Empire building of 1894. The oak is still alive: photographs from January 2015 and visitors in 2018 show it standing on the lawn.

No written source names its species, though photographs show a live oak. Nobody has published its age, girth or height either. If you know any of them, tell us.

The lawn is open ground on the town square, with no ticket to buy.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the state historical marker standing beside it. It stands on the north lawn of the Goliad County Courthouse, on the town square.

name: Rio Frio Landmark Oak

location.address: FM 1120, Rio Frio, Real County, TX 78879 (east side of the Rio Frio, about 7 miles south of Leakey)

access: VIEW ONLY. The oak stands on private property behind a hedge and fence with no-trespassing signs; it can be seen from the road (FM 1120) and a landmark plaque (erected by the Friends of the Rio Frio Oak) stands by it. Visitors must not enter the land. A good view of the trunk is difficult.
transport: Car only; remote Hill Country hamlet, about 7 miles (11 km) south of Leakey on FM 1120.
story:
When Rio Frio was laid out, sometime between 1880 and 1890, the village took its bearings from two landmarks: Schoolhouse Mountain to the east and this live oak to the west. That is the account retold by local history writers rather than a survey anyone has quoted. Backroads of Texas adds that the schoolhouse and part of the settlement were built in its shade.

Some travel sites go further and call it the third largest live oak in Texas, behind the Goose Island Oak and the Columbus Oak. Nobody has published a measurement to back that up, so it stays a claim, repeated rather than proven. The same gap runs through everything else: no age, girth or height has been recorded for it anywhere. If you know any of them, tell us.

It is still alive. Texas Escapes described it in 2001 and again in 2006, and a photograph dated 3 July 2024 shows it standing.

This is a tree to look at from the road, not to walk up to. It grows on private land behind a hedge and a fence posted with no-trespassing signs, and a good view of the trunk is hard to get. You see it from FM 1120 on the east side of the Rio Frio, about seven miles south of Leakey, where a plaque put up by the Friends of the Rio Frio Oak stands by the tree. Stay on the road; the land is not open.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque of the Friends of the Rio Frio Oak standing by it. It stands behind a hedge and a fence with no-trespassing signs on FM 1120, about seven miles south of Leakey, seen from the road only.
